activities.caption: file each habit — before 1600 or after
activities.name: hsBeforeBuckets

config.prompt: Two ways of knowing — file each habit:

items.label: Aristotle's physics: heavy bodies seek their natural place
Ptolemy's astronomy: Earth central, spheres carrying planets
experiments occasional and disreputable — 'mechanical arts' were for artisans
disagreements settled by citing authorities or spinning syllogisms
the telescope: anyone with a tube could check the heavens
the Royal Society's nullius in verba — take nobody's word for it

config.why: The old system explained, predicted and organised — its weakness was structural: knowledge did not compound. Islamic, Indian and Chinese scholars had run ahead on parts of the programme long before Europe assembled the delivery system.

activities.anchor: The transformation came as a package
activities.caption: line up the pieces, earliest first
activities.name: hsPiecesOrder

config.prompt: The method revolution, piece by piece — order them, earliest first:
items: the telescope reaches Galileo; the Sidereus Nuncius reports moons around Jupiter — 1608–1610
Bacon's Novum Organum argues for systematic experiment and induction — 1620
Galileo's inclined planes replace authority about falling bodies with numbers — 1638
the Royal Society makes publishing and priority-sharing a norm — 1660
config.why: Each piece had precedents; the novelty was their assembly into a cumulative machine — instruments, measurement, method statements, institutions and mathematics.

activities.anchor: The unification's audacity is the point
activities.caption: bet before you read on — why 1758 matters
activities.name: hsCometPredict

config.q: Halley's comet returned in 1758, predicted on Newton's theory. Why does that date matter?
choices: It was the comet's first recorded appearance
It is belief commanded by prediction: the same inverse-square law that explained falling apples predicted a return nobody had yet measured
Halley discovered the comet that year
config.why: A good theory does not just explain — it commands belief by predicting what nobody has yet measured. The Earth's oblate shape and the precession of the equinoxes were confirmed the same way.

activities.anchor: The nineteenth century rebuilt science as an institution
activities.caption: pair each institution with its work
activities.name: hsCareerMatch

config.prompt: Science becomes a career — pair each institution with its work:

pairs.right: trained students in cohorts — the laboratory as a teaching factory
hardens through the century as journals professionalise

pairs.left: the German dye and electrical industries
pairs.right: grow out of university chemistry and physics — the second industrial revolution

config.why: Science stopped being what gentlemen did and became what careers were made of — with everything that implies about who could enter.

activities.anchor: The Second World War merged science with the state
activities.caption: call the scale — research at its biggest
activities.name: hsManhattanEstimate

config.prompt: The Manhattan Project employed roughly how many people?
config.why: Some 130,000 people, several secret cities, one goal — organised research demonstrated it could move history; the LHC's discovery papers still rest on the 1660s contract of publishing and testing, executed by collaborations the size of towns.
config.context: Radar's MIT Radiation Laboratory — thousands of physicists — built the electronics industry's pedigree; NASA and CERN followed.

activities.anchor: Historians have complicated the neat version
activities.caption: line up the shift, earliest first
activities.name: hsRevolutionsOrder

config.prompt: Heliocentrism, gradual and contested — order the shift, earliest first:
items: Copernicus received as a better calendar calculation, not a cosmological manifesto — 1543
Galileo's telescope makes the heavens checkable — 1610
Newton's mechanics make the system irresistible — 1687
config.why: Revolutions are gradual, contested and local — the pattern is new instruments, new mathematics, and a young generation with careers to make, argued out in journals rather than decided by any single genius moment.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — who really did it
activities.name: hsGreatMenCloze

config.text: The record shows systems: Newton's calculus was invented simultaneously by %%0%%; Darwin co-published with %%1%%; the double helix ran on %%2%%'s X-ray data and a lab ecosystem.
config.hint: Genius is real and unevenly distributed — but the engine is the institutional machinery, and the machinery is what was historically rare.

activities.anchor: Before the telescope, the revolution needed a press
activities.caption: drag the divider — manuscript versus print
activities.name: hsPrintCompare

config.prompt: What a claim could be — drag the divider:

before.label: manuscript
before.text: Every copy an interpretation: errors unique and drifting; Euclid's geometrical figures hand-copied into guesswork for a millennium; a library a royal collector hoarded.

after.label: print
after.text: Identical copies — errors shared and correctable; diagrams and tables reproduced exactly; a library on a scholar's shelf, with title pages claiming priority and errata lists correcting shared mistakes.

config.why: Print was neutral about truth — it spread errors just as efficiently. The revolution was in what a claim could be: checkable by anyone holding the same page.
